overview: Momo’s settings tune broom movement, ranged attacks, and the camera used when aiming.
technicalOverview: Momo Nishimiya (CP_180) is a selectable Jujutsu Sorcerer built around a flying broom: a boosted, Jump-held dash, a held second normal attack, an aimed ranged beam, and a broom follow-up attack. Her AGameCharacter unique data lives in six populated rows of CharacterUniqueDataTable4, reached by zero-based row index through CharacterDataTable.Id_CharacterUnique; they are not AGameShikigami / ShikigamiUniqueDataTable data, and CP_180 has no trap or shikigami unique row. The numbers tune movement and camera behaviour rather than base stats. CP_180 has its own UCP_180_ActionController and UCP_180_BehaviorController over the shared base controllers, and reads these rows through the shared FGameCharacterAction::GetOwnerUniqueFloat / AGameCharacter::GetCharacterUniqueFloatValue helpers, which are unchecked float-array dereferences. No character-specific .inl file is included by the CP_180 sources; the only inline helper is the shared GameCharacterActionInline.h, which these code paths do not call. Descriptions below separate reads traced in CP_180's code from generic readers that merely exist in shared code.

CP_180.title: Momo's core movement and dash-gauge tuning
CP_180.overview: The main block for Momo Nishimiya's jump-hover, boosted dash and dash-gauge recovery. It is read often while she is airborne; while she is on the ground, two of its values are deliberately replaced by a fixed 1.0. A few generic systems also read the first three values.

0.label: Airborne dash-gauge refill speed
0.simple: How quickly the dash gauge fills again while Momo is in the air; on the ground this number is ignored.
0.technical: UCP_180_ActionController::GetDashGaugeRecoverInterpSpeed returns 1.0 when GetGroundTraceHit()==1 (grounded), otherwise UniqueRows[0]->FloatValue[0]. AGameCharacter::GetActionValue99 forwards it to the status controller, which calls Interp1B0.Update(Value * DeltaTime) to advance the gauge-refill interpolation. The read is an unchecked array dereference. Generic readers of (0,0) also exist (secondary-target steering divisor, projection-sorcery receive restraint-time fallback, AI hold-node durations), but no CP_180 action was traced to those nodes, so they are noted rather than treated as Momo-specific effects.

1.label: Airborne dash-gauge wait rate
1.simple: How fast the short pause before the air gauge starts refilling counts down; grounded characters use a fixed rate instead.
1.technical: UCP_180_ActionController::GetDashGaugeRecoverWaitRate returns 1.0 when GetGroundTraceHit()==1, otherwise FloatValue[1] of row 0. AGameCharacter::GetActionValue100 passes it to UGameCharacterStatusController::Tick: DashGaugeRecoverWait = max(wait - Rate*DeltaTime, 0). When the wait reaches <= 0 the refill interpolation starts (unless the DashGaugeNotRecoverItem buff is active).

2.label: Jump-hold hover gauge drain
2.simple: Dash gauge spent per second by holding Jump to hover: with the stick still in a jump, or with the stick moving in a running jump.
2.technical: FCP_180_Jump::Tick and FCP_180_RunJump::Tick pass FloatValue[2] of row 0 to GetNormalDashGaugeCost while Jump is held and the respective stick test passes (stick exactly zero for Jump, stick size > 0 for RunJump). The helper multiplies by the owner's normal dash gauge consume rate (0 while unlimited gauge); that cost is multiplied by DeltaTime, subtracted from DashGauge, clamped to [0, max], and the hold ends when the gauge reaches 0. 360 is the base cost before that multiplier; no other conversion is done in the traced code.

3.label: Boosted dash start-up gauge cost
3.simple: One-time dash-gauge fee for starting a dash with Jump held (Momo's boosted dash).
3.technical: FCP_180_NormalDash::GetBoostGaugeCost passes FloatValue[3] of row 0 to GetNormalDashGaugeCost. It is applied on a fresh Jump press when no JumpCount / RunJumpLimitWithoutHitPointMax / DashStepJumpLimit vow is active; otherwise the dash becomes a penalty dash and this cost is not charged. The result is subtracted from DashGauge with a floor of 0. The value 0 therefore means no upfront fee at the default rate, not that the entry is unused.

4.label: Boosted dash gauge drain per second
4.simple: Dash gauge drained each second while the Jump-boosted dash keeps going.
4.technical: FCP_180_NormalDash::GetBoostDrainRate passes FloatValue[4] of row 0 to GetNormalDashGaugeCost; 330 is the base before the dash-gauge consume-rate multiplier (which is 0 with unlimited gauge). While bBoostActive is set, Tick subtracts DrainRate*DeltaTime from DashGauge, clamped to [0, max]. This is a recurring cost, separate from the start-up cost in value 3.

5.label: Boosted dash extra continuation window
5.simple: A short grace period, in seconds, that keeps a boosted dash going after the ordinary dash would stop.
5.technical: FCP_180_NormalDash::IsDashContinuing first asks the base dash; if that says stop, but bBoostActive==1 and FloatValue[5] of row 0 > BoostTime, it still returns true. BoostTime accumulates DeltaTime only while the boost is active and resets to 0 whenever the held-Jump state changes. The comparison is strict (>), so a 0.4-second window lapses once BoostTime reaches 0.4.

notes.text: The two recovery values in this row matter in the air: the controller returns a literal 1.0 on the ground, so editing them changes airborne gauge recovery only. Both overrides were verified byte-identical to retail in the reconstruction record.

CP_180_ATTACKC.title: AttackC combo-step hold timing
CP_180_ATTACKC.overview: Two short timers that govern how long Momo holds her broom in her second normal attack and how long she may stay grounded before the follow-up animation takes over.

0.label: AttackC hold duration
0.simple: How long the AttackC step can be held before it moves into the next animation.
0.technical: In TCP_180_NormalAttack_2::TickAttack (used by the ground and air NormalAttack_2 actions), when the action's start count is zero the phase-1/2 branch advances to phase 4 if a hit, guard or flag is set OR FloatValue[0] of row 1 <= ActionElapsedTime. Phase 3 continues to wait only while FloatValue[0] > ActionElapsedTime. Thus 0.3 s is an inclusive finishing boundary for the hold; these timers are only accumulated in this custom branch, not when the start count is nonzero.

1.label: Grounded wait limit
1.simple: Extra time on the ground before the held AttackC step is cut short.
1.technical: Phase 3 keeps holding only while all of: no hit, no guard, no flag, FloatValue[0] > ActionElapsedTime and FloatValue[1] > GroundedWaitElapsed. GroundedWaitElapsed is zeroed on entering phase 3 and grows by DeltaTime there; the `>` comparisons mean 0.1 s is exclusive for the wait. Reaching the limit plays AttackC_01_02 on body and weapon and moves to phase 4.

CP_180_ATTACKF.title: AttackF finisher row (no float reader found)
CP_180_ATTACKF.overview: Momo's third normal attack finisher has a unique row with two nonzero numbers, but no code path in the reconstructed CP_180 sources or shared base actions reads them. The AttackF attack-set changeover uses a different table entirely.

0.label: AttackF first value (unresolved)
0.simple: A 0.5 stored on the AttackF finisher row; no on-screen effect could be traced to it.
0.technical: No GetOwnerUniqueFloat or GetCharacterUniqueFloatValue call with ValueIndex 0 and RowIndex 2 appears in any CP_180 source or in the shared base action/controller code reachable from its action factory. The nearby (0,2) read found in FGameTrapAction reads the trap's source character, and CP_180's controller creates no trap. The AttackF name here only matches an AttackSet row swapped in by the passive stack; that is a different data table. Status is unresolved, not proof that retail never reads this value.

1.label: AttackF second value (unresolved)
1.simple: A 2 stored on the same AttackF finisher row; no consumer was identified.
1.technical: No call reading ValueIndex 1 of row 2 was found in the CP_180 action or behaviour controllers, nor in the shared base actions they instantiate. A shared (1,2) read exists only inside trap code, and CP_180 has no trap forwarding. The 2 must not be interpreted as a shot count or level merely from its size; its meaning is unresolved.

notes.text: This is the only populated Momo unique row without a traced float reader. Reused row names can have different consumers on other characters, so no behaviour was borrowed from another character's ATTACKF row.

CP_180_ATTACKG.title: Cursed Energy 1 (AttackG) beam-aim steering
CP_180_ATTACKG.overview: The aiming rules for Momo's first cursed-energy attack, the ranged broom beam: how long it can be held, its left/right and up/down limits, and how quickly the stick moves the aim. Later uses turn faster and drop the first-use yaw clamp.

0.label: First beam hold time
0.simple: Maximum time she can hold the beam on its first use.
0.technical: FCP_180_CursedEnergyAttack_1::TickAttack, only in the Count==1 case, adds DeltaTime to ActionElapsedTime while the CursedEnergyAttack_1 key is held and ActionElapsedTime < FloatValue[0] of row 3. If the key is released or elapsed time reaches 0.5, the finish flags are set. This value is not consulted in the Count>=2 branch of this function.

1.label: First-use yaw range
1.simple: How far left and right the beam can be pointed on its first use; the value is halved for each side.
1.technical: HalfYawLimit = FloatValue[1] of row 3 * 0.5 (60 -> 30 degrees per side). For Count < 2 the accumulated YawOffset is clamped with FMath::Clamp(..., -HalfYawLimit, +HalfYawLimit), so both endpoints are allowed. For Count >= 2 the clamp is skipped and yaw keeps accumulating.

2.label: Beam downward pitch limit
2.simple: Maximum downward angle of the beam aim.
2.technical: Lower = FloatValue[2] of row 3. AimPitch = FMath::Clamp(AimPitch - Speed*Stick.Y, -Lower, Upper), so value 15 allows down to -15 degrees; clamp endpoints are inclusive. The resulting pitch drives AnimInstance FullBodyRotation.Roll and AimDirection.

3.label: Beam upward pitch limit
3.simple: Maximum upward angle of the beam aim.
3.technical: Upper = FloatValue[3] of row 3; the same inclusive clamp caps AimPitch at +40 degrees with this data. Both pitch limits are read every tick while aiming is active.

4.label: Beam steering speed
4.simple: How fast the stick swings the beam, measured as degrees per second at full stick deflection.
4.technical: Speed = FloatValue[4] of row 3 * DeltaTime (80 -> 80 degrees per second per full stick). It is multiplied by Stick.X for YawOffset and subtracted times Stick.Y for AimPitch on every aiming tick.

5.label: Later-use steering multiplier
5.simple: Aim turns twice as fast on the second and later beam uses.
5.technical: When the action's start count is >= 2, Speed *= FloatValue[5] of row 3 (2 doubles the per-frame yaw and pitch step). The same start-count test also removes the first-use yaw clamp, so these two effects combine on later activations.

notes.text: The beam follow-up dash is picked by cursed-energy level: CP_180_ATTACKG_1 / _2 / _3 in ActionDashDataTables, falling back to the current dash row if not found. This is a different table from the unique row; the beam camera itself always uses the fixed unique row 4.

CP_180_ATTACKG_SHOOT_CAMERA.title: Cursed Energy 1 beam-aim camera
CP_180_ATTACKG_SHOOT_CAMERA.overview: The camera used during Momo's aimed broom beam (Cursed Energy 1 / AttackG): a high, far-back view with wide FOV, symmetric gaze limits, and a small orbit. The shared request builder reads the first eleven values of this row whenever the attack starts aiming.

0.label: Camera offset along gaze-forward
0.simple: Moves the camera -180 units along its gaze-forward axis in this shot.
0.technical: MakeUniqueCameraRequest(2, 4) reads FloatValue[0] of row 4 into FVirtualCameraRequest.CameraOffset.X. UpdateRequestCamera rotates that offset by the gaze rotation and adds it to the eye base, then traces toward the gaze for collision. This helper's CameraMode argument 2 means 'build the request from a unique-float row', not virtual-camera mode 2.

1.label: Camera sideways offset
1.simple: Moves the camera -150 units along its gaze-local sideways axis.
1.technical: FloatValue[1] of row 4 becomes CameraOffset.Y in the same MakeUniqueCameraRequest(2, 4) call; it is part of the offset vector rotated into world space by the gaze rotation.

2.label: Camera height offset
2.simple: Raises or lowers the camera 100 units relative to the eye base in this shot.
2.technical: FloatValue[2] of row 4 becomes CameraOffset.Z. Positive values place the camera above the eye base, negative below it, before the gaze-space rotation is applied. This value is read even when it is zero.

3.label: Largest downward gaze angle
3.simple: Limits how far below the eye the camera may look (80 degrees here).
3.technical: FloatValue[3] of row 4 becomes Request.LimitAngleDown. In UpdateRequestCamera, if the gaze lies below the eye base and its elevation exceeds this limit (strict >), the gaze is rotated back by LimitAngleDown. The comparison uses angle-in-degrees.

4.label: Largest upward gaze angle
4.simple: Limits how far above the eye the camera may look (80 degrees here).
4.technical: FloatValue[4] of row 4 becomes Request.LimitAngleUp, applied symmetrically when the gaze is above the eye base and elevation is strictly greater than the limit.

5.label: Field of view during the shot
5.simple: Sets a field of view of 110 while this attack's camera is active.
5.technical: FloatValue[5] of row 4 becomes Request.FieldOfView (110). SetCameraMode only starts an FOV interpolation when this number is > 0; the restore requests in CP_180's action code use a literal 90.0 instead, so this value governs the aiming view, not the return view.

6.label: Field-of-view blend time
6.simple: How many seconds the view takes to zoom into and out of this shot (0.25 s).
6.technical: FloatValue[6] of row 4 becomes Request.FieldOfViewBlendTime. Positive values start FovInterp from the current FOV to the requested FOV with the easing selected by value 7; zero or negative makes the FOV snap. Momo's action code also reads this same value directly when restoring to a 90.0 FOV, so it affects both entering and leaving the shot.

7.label: Field-of-view easing choice
7.simple: Selects smooth-in-out easing (3) for the zoom.
7.technical: FloatValue[7] of row 4 is cast to int in MakeUniqueCameraRequest: 0 = Linear, 1 = EaseIn, 2 = EaseOut, 3 = EaseInOut; any other value leaves the freshly built request's default Linear. The current 3 selects EaseInOut for FovInterp.

8.label: Gaze orbit yaw
8.simple: Turns the gaze 10 degrees around the camera after the camera is placed.
8.technical: FloatValue[8] of row 4 becomes Request.OrbitYaw. UpdateRequestCamera builds FRotator(OrbitPitch, OrbitYaw, 0) and applies it to the gaze only when the rotator is nonzero; zero in the attack-H row means no horizontal orbit.

9.label: Gaze orbit pitch
9.simple: Tilts the gaze -10 degrees around the camera.
9.technical: FloatValue[9] of row 4 becomes Request.OrbitPitch, the Pitch member of the orbit rotator used in UpdateRequestCamera when the orbit is nonzero.

10.label: Camera roll
10.technical: FloatValue[10] of row 4 becomes Request.Roll and is passed to SetViewTarget87 as the roll argument. It is not part of the orbit rotator and does not affect the collision trace or gaze clamp.

notes.text: The camera is switched to virtual-camera mode 3 at the beam notify (IntParameter 10), where Mode3GazeLocation is fed from the beam aim direction each tick; leaving the attack restores the saved mode with a literal 90.0 FOV and this row's blend time.

CP_180_ATTACKH_SHOOT_CAMERA.title: Cursed Energy 2 broom-attack camera
CP_180_ATTACKH_SHOOT_CAMERA.overview: The camera used by Momo's second cursed-energy attack (AttackH): a much lower, closer view with tighter gaze limits than the beam camera. Its first eleven values feed the same shared request builder on the first homing start, and value 6 is reused when the view is restored.

0.label: Camera offset along gaze-forward
0.simple: Moves the camera -130 units along its gaze-forward axis in this shot.
0.technical: MakeUniqueCameraRequest(2, 5) reads FloatValue[0] of row 5 into FVirtualCameraRequest.CameraOffset.X. UpdateRequestCamera rotates that offset by the gaze rotation and adds it to the eye base, then traces toward the gaze for collision. This helper's CameraMode argument 2 means 'build the request from a unique-float row', not virtual-camera mode 2.

1.label: Camera sideways offset
1.simple: Moves the camera 67 units along its gaze-local sideways axis.
1.technical: FloatValue[1] of row 5 becomes CameraOffset.Y in the same MakeUniqueCameraRequest(2, 5) call; it is part of the offset vector rotated into world space by the gaze rotation.

2.label: Camera height offset
2.simple: Raises or lowers the camera -10 units relative to the eye base in this shot.
2.technical: FloatValue[2] of row 5 becomes CameraOffset.Z. Positive values place the camera above the eye base, negative below it, before the gaze-space rotation is applied. This value is read even when it is zero.

3.label: Largest downward gaze angle
3.simple: Limits how far below the eye the camera may look (30 degrees here).
3.technical: FloatValue[3] of row 5 becomes Request.LimitAngleDown. In UpdateRequestCamera, if the gaze lies below the eye base and its elevation exceeds this limit (strict >), the gaze is rotated back by LimitAngleDown. The comparison uses angle-in-degrees.

4.label: Largest upward gaze angle
4.simple: Limits how far above the eye the camera may look (30 degrees here).
4.technical: FloatValue[4] of row 5 becomes Request.LimitAngleUp, applied symmetrically when the gaze is above the eye base and elevation is strictly greater than the limit.

5.label: Field of view during the shot
5.simple: Sets a field of view of 110 while this attack's camera is active.
5.technical: FloatValue[5] of row 5 becomes Request.FieldOfView (110). SetCameraMode only starts an FOV interpolation when this number is > 0; the restore requests in CP_180's action code use a literal 90.0 instead, so this value governs the aiming view, not the return view.

6.label: Field-of-view blend time
6.simple: How many seconds the view takes to zoom into and out of this shot (0.35 s).
6.technical: FloatValue[6] of row 5 becomes Request.FieldOfViewBlendTime. Positive values start FovInterp from the current FOV to the requested FOV with the easing selected by value 7; zero or negative makes the FOV snap. Momo's action code also reads this same value directly when restoring to a 90.0 FOV, so it affects both entering and leaving the shot.

7.label: Field-of-view easing choice
7.simple: Selects smooth-in-out easing (3) for the zoom.
7.technical: FloatValue[7] of row 5 is cast to int in MakeUniqueCameraRequest: 0 = Linear, 1 = EaseIn, 2 = EaseOut, 3 = EaseInOut; any other value leaves the freshly built request's default Linear. The current 3 selects EaseInOut for FovInterp.

8.label: Gaze orbit yaw
8.simple: Turns the gaze 0 degrees around the camera after the camera is placed.
8.technical: FloatValue[8] of row 5 becomes Request.OrbitYaw. UpdateRequestCamera builds FRotator(OrbitPitch, OrbitYaw, 0) and applies it to the gaze only when the rotator is nonzero; zero in the attack-H row means no horizontal orbit.

9.label: Gaze orbit pitch
9.simple: Tilts the gaze -3 degrees around the camera.
9.technical: FloatValue[9] of row 5 becomes Request.OrbitPitch, the Pitch member of the orbit rotator used in UpdateRequestCamera when the orbit is nonzero.

10.label: Camera roll
10.technical: FloatValue[10] of row 5 becomes Request.Roll and is passed to SetViewTarget87 as the roll argument. It is not part of the orbit rotator and does not affect the collision trace or gaze clamp.

notes.text: Unlike the beam camera, this request is applied through SetCameraMode(2, ...) on the first homing start, and it is restored only while the camera is still in mode 2 when the attack finishes; the restore again uses 90.0 FOV plus this row's blend time.

Holding Jump turns Momo's dash into a boosted dash: a one-time gauge fee, a per-second drain, a surface splash, and a 0.4 s grace window keyed to the last Jump-state change. Jump-limit binding vows replace it with a penalty dash instead, so the fee and boost effects are skipped.

Airborne dash-gauge recovery is unusual for her: the controller overrides two base getters so air recovery uses row 0 values 0 and 1, while grounded characters get a hard 1.0. Those overrides are the only ones of their slots in the reconstructed binary.

The aimed beam's second and third activations use a cursed-energy-level-specific ActionDash row, add the CP_180 passive buff, and steer twice as fast without the first-use yaw clamp. The passive itself also swaps several normal-attack sets (B_2, E_2, F_2).

Two camera rows use the same shared builder with different row indices: row 4 for the beam's mode-3 gaze camera and row 5 for the broom attack's mode-2 camera. The builder's '2' argument selects 'make request from unique floats'; the SetCameraMode call then uses mode 3 or 2. Both restore with a hard-coded 90.0 field of view but keep the row's blend time.

Momo's behaviour controller only specialises AI ordinals 0x03, 0x04, 0x05, 0x0e and 0x11 (jump/air-jump/dash-jump mobility plus two attacks); all other ordinals forward to the parent factory. The generic timed CursedEnergyAttack hold nodes that read unique row 0 values are built by CP_040's controller, not hers.

Surface tracing gives Momo water-specific jump, dash and landing effects, and the CP_180 passive attaches/removes waist effects; none of this reads unique floats, but it explains why the same jump/dash code has extra sound and effect branches around the gauge-tuning reads.

Both unique-float hops are plain unchecked dereferences, so an out-of-range row or value index would be invalid memory access rather than a safe fallback. Verification notes document that retail keeps these as calls at cold sites while some hot sites inline them; that is an emission detail, not a different data lookup.
